shots.phrase: Begin by framing Foundations of Computation as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results.
Consider this worked case: A finite automaton accepts the string 'abab' by transitioning through states that track alternating 'a' and 'b' characters.
List the givens before choosing a method, because an unstated assumption can change the conclusion.
Now define Formal Languages and Grammars precisely enough that another learner could test the definition.
Consider this worked case: A context-free grammar defines valid arithmetic expressions by recursively combining terms and operators.
Separate the formal definition from an implementation detail, then identify what evidence would distinguish them.
With the foundation in place, examine how Automata Theory Basics operates in a concrete sequence.
Consider this worked case: A pushdown automaton recognizes nested parentheses by pushing symbols onto a stack and popping them during matching.
Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition.
Next, compare the choices involved in Computability Limits and make the decision criteria explicit.
Consider this worked case: The halting problem demonstrates that no general algorithm can decide whether an arbitrary program will eventually stop.
Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts.
Apply Complexity and Resource Bounds to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition.
Consider this worked case: A sorting algorithm with O(n log n) time complexity processes larger inputs more efficiently than O(n^2) alternatives.
Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step.
Examine the tradeoffs in Loop Invariants and Proofs, including what improves and what becomes more difficult.
Consider this worked case: In a binary search, the invariant states that the target value, if present, lies within the current search interval.
State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable.
Stress-test the reasoning around Divide-and-Conquer Strategy with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome.
Consider this worked case: Merge sort splits an array into halves, recursively sorts each half, and merges the sorted halves into a complete sorted array.
Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds.
Use Recurrence Relations to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action.
Consider this worked case: The recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) describes the time complexity of merge sort, solving to O(n log n).
Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause.
Connect Graph Algorithms and Reachability to the earlier ideas and explain how the pieces work as one system.
Consider this worked case: Breadth-first search finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph by exploring neighbors level by level.
Explain each connection explicitly and verify that information retains the same meaning across representations.
Finish with Practical Analysis Checklist as a practical checklist that can guide a new analysis.
Consider this worked case: Before implementing a sorting routine, verify the preconditions, prove the loop invariant, and derive the recurrence for time bounds.
For each checklist item, record the evidence, the remaining uncertainty, and the next verification step.
